headline_en: Is Bangladesh ready for expatriate voting?
summary_en: An opinion column (10 Oct 2025) argues that Bangladesh is rushing into expatriate (probashi) voting. It reports the Election Commission plan to pilot voting by Bangladeshis abroad in Saudi Arabia, Malaysia, the UAE and the UK through embassy booths after online registration, gives estimates of Bangladeshi populations in those countries, and lists risks such as registration and verification problems, vote-buying under the kafala sponsorship system, and the lack of a specific law.

facts.statement: As of October 2025, Bangladesh's Election Commission (EC) has said it plans to start expatriate voting on a pilot basis in Saudi Arabia, Malaysia, the United Arab Emirates and the United Kingdom.
facts.source_in_article: Election Commission, as reported in the column

facts.statement: Under the EC plan reported in October 2025, in the first phase voting would be at booths in Bangladesh embassies: voters would first register online, and on the set day would vote after their passport and NID (national ID) are verified.
facts.source_in_article: Election Commission plan, as reported in the column

facts.statement: As of October 2025, no detailed announcement had been made on foreign government approval, security protocols or server set-up for expatriate voting; the columnists note the election schedule (tofshil) is to be announced in December.
The column states there are about 25 lakh (2.5 million) Bangladeshi expatriates in Saudi Arabia.
The column states there are about 12 lakh Bangladeshi expatriates in Malaysia.
The column states there are about 10 lakh Bangladeshi expatriates in the United Arab Emirates.
The column states there are about 5 lakh Bangladeshi expatriates in the United Kingdom.
The column gives the number of Bangladeshis living in various countries as about 1 crore 30 lakh (13 million); a subheading elsewhere in the article refers to 'one and a half crore' expatriates.
According to the column, expatriates sent USD 7.59 billion in remittances in the first three months of 2025, and Bangladesh is the sixth largest remittance-receiving country in the world.
About 13 crore NIDs have been issued in Bangladesh, but there is no updated database tracking whether holders live abroad, according to the column.
The columnists say the biggest obstacle at the registration stage is duplication and verification, because passport, NID and birth registration are held in three separate systems.

The columnists warn that in the Middle East, where workers are under the sponsor or 'kafala' system, creating conditions for expatriates to vote freely will be harder; experts from Sri Lanka and the Philippines have warned that many expatriate voters at one address raise risks of vote-buying, coercion, or influence through politically appointed mission officials.
facts.source_in_article: Columnists; Sri Lankan and Philippine experts

facts.statement: Bangladesh has not yet passed a clear law on expatriate voting; under Article 122 of the Constitution voting rights depend on citizenship, but the legal position of those permanently settled abroad is unclear, the column says. The columnists propose a separate 'Probashi Vote Ain 2025' (Expatriate Voting Act 2025) with strict penalties for fake registration or undue influence.

Unanswered questions listed by the column: whether people who register abroad will stay on the voter list at home, what happens to people who gave up their Bangladeshi passport abroad but still have a voter number, and how a voter abroad will know and vote for the candidates in their own constituency under the current symbol-based paper ballot system.

Comparisons given by the column: in India, of 1.2 lakh registered overseas voters only 2,958 voted in the 2024 election because they must return home to vote; in the Philippines fewer than 15% of over 10 million overseas citizens register and only 20% of those vote; in Pennsylvania (USA) ballots of more than 4,000 overseas voters were challenged.

The columnists recommend embassy/consulate in-person voting (which they say most of the UK Bangladeshi community favours), strict verification with annual renewal, a simple online registration system, an independent oversight committee with international observers, and voter education for expatriates.

headline_en: Denmark tightens rules: international students' rights to work and bring family limited
summary_en: Denmark's Ministry of Immigration and Integration announced in an 18 September (2025) notice stricter rules for non-EU (third-country) students, aimed particularly at students from Bangladesh and Nepal who it says used student visas as a backdoor into the labour market. Measures include stricter academic requirements, document checks, review of past residence permits for fraud, limits on bringing family, cutting the post-study work permit from three years to one, higher tuition and monitoring of agents. The article also gives statistics on family accompaniment, dropout and pass rates of Bangladeshi students.

facts.statement: Denmark's Ministry of Immigration and Integration said in a notice on 18 September that university admission rules for third-country (non-EU) students will be made stricter, and that it will now be 'much harder for those without the necessary qualifications to study at Danish universities'; the measure targets in particular students from Bangladesh and Nepal entering the labour market through student visas.
facts.source_in_article: Danish Ministry of Immigration and Integration notice (18 September), as reported

facts.statement: Under Denmark's new policy (announced September 2025), the post-study work permit for international students is cut from three years to one year.
facts.source_in_article: Danish Ministry of Immigration and Integration notice (18 September), as reported

facts.statement: Under Denmark's new policy (September 2025), international students' ability to bring a spouse or dependants will be reduced.
facts.source_in_article: Danish Ministry of Immigration and Integration notice (18 September), as reported

facts.statement: Under Denmark's new policy (September 2025), third-country students may have to sit a university admission test or pass a specific language test.
facts.source_in_article: Danish Ministry of Immigration and Integration notice (18 September), as reported

facts.statement: Under Denmark's new policy (September 2025), universities must strictly verify students' academic documents with the help of the National ID Centre.
facts.source_in_article: Danish Ministry of Immigration and Integration notice (18 September), as reported

facts.statement: Denmark will review residence permits previously granted to Bangladeshi and Nepali students for possible fraud, under the policy announced in September 2025.
facts.source_in_article: Danish Ministry of Immigration and Integration notice (18 September), as reported

facts.statement: Under Denmark's new policy (September 2025), universities must follow new rules to prevent admission through agents and fake documents, and monitoring of agents will be increased to stop Denmark being promoted as an easy-residence country.
facts.source_in_article: Danish Ministry of Immigration and Integration notice (18 September), as reported

facts.statement: Denmark will raise tuition fees for international students so that fewer applications come from cost-sensitive countries, under the policy announced in September 2025 (no amount given).
facts.source_in_article: Danish Ministry of Immigration and Integration notice (18 September), as reported

facts.statement: Denmark says it will support skilled and academically strong students under its new policy (September 2025).
facts.source_in_article: Danish Ministry of Immigration and Integration notice (18 September), as reported

facts.statement: Between 2022 and 2024, 74% of Nepali students, 58% of Bangladeshi students and 23% of Indian students brought family members to Denmark, compared with only 1% of Chinese and 2% of US students.

A survey by Aarhus University found one-third of Bangladeshi students were considered 'not study-oriented'; Bangladeshi first-year dropout was 13% against 4% for other international students, and Bangladeshi exam pass rates were 55-65% against 90% for students from other countries.
Denmark's policies were drawn up after analysing dropout and pass rates from eight Danish universities.
facts.source_in_article: Danish Ministry of Immigration and Integration notice (18 September), as reported

facts.statement: Kaare Dybvad Bek (named in the article as a former minister) said some people had unfortunately used student visas as a backdoor into the Danish labour market and that numbers of students and families from Bangladesh and Nepal had risen sharply in recent years.
Danish universities said many students are unfamiliar with group work and exam methods, creating academic challenges.

headline_en: Potential to raise exports to Malaysia held back by tariff barriers
summary_en: A business report on Bangladesh-Malaysia trade says high tariffs (20-30%) and the lack of a free trade agreement keep Bangladeshi exports to Malaysia low. It notes Malaysia is one of Bangladesh's main labour markets with over 8 lakh Bangladeshi workers, who make up over 38% of more than 21 lakh foreign workers there. FTA talks restarted after Chief Adviser Yunus's mid-August visit; formal talks may start in mid-2026.

facts.statement: Malaysia is one of Bangladesh's main labour markets, with more than 8 lakh Bangladeshi migrant workers working there, according to the report (September 2025).
According to Malaysia's statistics department as cited, Malaysia has about 3.5 crore people and more than 21 lakh foreign workers, of whom more than about 38% (over 8 lakh) are Bangladeshi.
facts.source_in_article: Department of Statistics Malaysia, as cited

facts.statement: Total Bangladesh-Malaysia bilateral trade is about USD 2.8 billion (280 crore dollars), of which Bangladesh exports only USD 250-300 million, 8-10% of the total; Bangladeshi exporters pay 20% up to 30% duty in Malaysia because there is no free trade agreement (FTA), while India, China and Pakistan have FTAs.

Bangladesh's high commission in Malaysia said Malaysia has FTAs with about 14 countries; FTA talks with Bangladesh restarted after Chief Adviser Muhammad Yunus visited Malaysia in mid-August (2025), a draft terms of reference for negotiations has been prepared, and acting High Commissioner (Deputy High Commissioner) Mosammat Shahanara Monica said formal talks could begin around mid-2026.
facts.source_in_article: Bangladesh High Commission in Malaysia; Mosammat Shahanara Monica

facts.statement: PRAN group sells food products in Malaysia through local supplier Pinnacle Foods; PRAN officials say the large number of Bangladeshi expatriates in Malaysia is a big opportunity for them.

headline_en: 66 people including women and children rescued while being trafficked to Malaysia
summary_en: A joint Coast Guard and Navy operation on 18 September 2025 rescued 66 people, 44 of them women and children and most of them Rohingya, gathered in a hideout in the deep hills of Kachchhopia, Baharchhara union, Teknaf (Cox's Bazar) for trafficking to Malaysia. Some were lured with promises of a better life in Malaysia, others abducted and held for ransom; 15-20 traffickers escaped.

facts.statement: On Thursday 18 September 2025, between 6 pm and 10 pm, a joint Coast Guard and Navy operation rescued 66 people gathered for trafficking to Malaysia from a hideout in the deep hills of Kachchhopia area, Baharchhara union, Teknaf upazila, Cox's Bazar; 44 of them were women and children, and most were Rohingya.
facts.source_in_article: Coast Guard; Lt Cdr Siam-ul-Haque, Coast Guard HQ media officer

facts.statement: Traffickers, helped by an organised broker (dalal) ring, gathered people at a hill hideout in Teknaf: some were lured with promises of a better life in Malaysia and others were abducted and held hostage while ransom was sought (September 2025).

During the 18 September 2025 Teknaf raid, 15 to 20 members of the trafficking gang escaped; the Coast Guard said efforts are under way to identify and arrest them, a case is being prepared at Teknaf police station, and the 66 rescued will be handed to relatives after identity checks.
facts.source_in_article: Coast Guard; Lt Cdr Siam-ul-Haque, Coast Guard HQ media officer

facts.statement: So far in 2025 (as of 19 September), 62 human traffickers have been arrested and 77 people rescued in Teknaf, according to law enforcement sources.
Human trafficking incidents occur more in the winter season, according to law enforcement sources cited for Teknaf.

headline_en: Alleged attempt to traffic three girls in Netrokona; two including a Chinese national detained
summary_en: Police detained Chinese national Li Oi Hao (32) and his associate Faridul Islam (34) of Kurigram in Kendua, Netrokona on 15 September 2025 on suspicion of human trafficking and rescued three girls. Li had married a 17-year-old garment worker on 1 September, promising to take her to China and to give her family 1 lakh taka; a friend of his married another 17-year-old on 14 September. Police found photos, voter IDs, passports and payment records of many girls on Faridul's phone.

facts.statement: At dawn on Monday 15 September 2025, police detained Chinese national Li Oi Hao (লি ওই হাও, 32) and his associate Faridul Islam (34), son of Abdul Hanif Mia of Sukhdeb Paschim Para, Rajarhat, Kurigram, in Kamalpur area of Kendua municipality, Netrokona, on suspicion of human trafficking, rescued three girls and seized a microbus.
facts.source_in_article: Netrokona Superintendent of Police Mirza Saem Mahmud; local residents and police

facts.statement: Method described: a Chinese man married a 17-year-old girl from Kamalpur, Kendua (a garment factory worker in Dhaka) on 1 September 2025 with a Bangladeshi associate's help, said he would take her to China on 20 September, and promised her family 1 lakh taka; a Chinese friend of his married a 17-year-old from Gopi Nadi, Melandaha, Jamalpur in Dhaka on 14 September, also saying he would take her to China; a 19-year-old from Gogda, Kendua was also promised a trip to China.

On the evening of 14 September 2025, local people in Kendua, suspicious of the two men, asked for their passport numbers and legal papers for staying in Bangladesh; when they could not show them, locals informed the Madan temporary army camp and Kendua police, who detained them the next dawn.

The Netrokona SP said Faridul Islam claimed to be a garment worker, but his phone held photos, voter IDs, passports and money-transaction records of many girls from various parts of Bangladesh; the ring is believed to have been involved in trafficking for a long time, targeting women from simple, poor rural families through brokers with various lures to traffic them to China. Investigation and legal action are under way.

headline_en: Attempt to grab Italy-based migrant's house in Keraniganj by claiming the land, vandalism
summary_en: Liton Howlader (45), who has lived in Italy for 17 years, returned to Keraniganj to save a house he built on land bought four years earlier, after a group led by alleged land grabber Alamgir Hossain claimed the land after 5 August 2024, evicted tenants on 31 August 2025 and began demolishing the house. A court case is pending with a hearing on 1 October; police say they received a written complaint.

facts.statement: Italy-based migrant Liton Howlader (45) of Kulchar, Shakta union, Keraniganj says that on the morning of 31 August 2025 Alamgir Hossain (36), Shahadat, Shahin and 30-35 others armed with local weapons forcibly entered his six-room semi-pucca house on 5.75 decimals of land in Madhyerchar mouza (Keraniganj Model police station area), attacked and evicted tenants, beat his younger brother Rafiqul and began demolishing the house despite a pending court case.

Liton Howlader, in Italy for 17 years, bought the land four years earlier with valid papers and pays land tax; after the 5 August (2024) political change, alleged land grabbers claimed it. His family filed a written complaint at Keraniganj Model police station and later a court case, with the next hearing on 1 October (2025). He returned from Italy about four days before his 8 September 2025 press conference and says he has received death threats.

Alamgir Hossain, who lives in Lalbagh, Dhaka, is accused of buying disputed land, occupying it and reselling it; he claims he bought land in the same plot (dag) and has valid papers, but could not explain why he made the claim only after 5 August.
Keraniganj Model police station officer-in-charge Monirul Haque said the station received a written complaint about the Italy-based migrant's land and would take necessary action after inquiry.

headline_en: 30 more Bangladeshis sent back from the United States
summary_en: Thirty Bangladeshis (29 men, one woman) deported from the US for living without valid documents landed at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport, Dhaka, around 12:15 am on the night of Thursday 4 September 2025. They were handcuffed on the plane; SB says 187 Bangladeshis have been returned so far amid Trump's second-term crackdown.

facts.statement: Thirty Bangladeshis (29 men and one woman) deported from the United States for living without valid documents arrived at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport, Dhaka, on a plane that landed around 12:15 am on the night of Thursday 4 September 2025.

Since Donald Trump began his second term as US president and stepped up operations against undocumented migrants, 187 Bangladeshis in total have been sent back as of 5 September 2025, according to SB sources.
Bangladesh foreign ministry officials say only people who have lost their legal battles in the US are being sent back, and the ministry is informed in advance about those being deported.
The 30 Bangladeshis were put on the plane in handcuffs in the US and kept handcuffed on board; the handcuffs were removed after landing in Dhaka, they told law enforcement.

headline_en: Why is the price of the dream abroad so high?
summary_en: A short reader opinion piece says migrant workers going to Saudi Arabia, Malaysia or other Middle East countries often borrow several lakh taka because of legal and illegal broker chains, face lower pay and harsh conditions than promised, and suffer stress, illness, accidents and suicide, leaving families with debt. It calls for worker safety, transparent recruitment and debt-free migration.

facts.statement: Because of legal and illegal broker (dalal) chains, a worker going to Saudi Arabia, Malaysia or another Middle East country often has to borrow several lakh taka, raising it by selling land, taking high-interest loans or using all savings, according to the opinion piece.
The piece says brokers promise large salaries but many workers in reality face low wages, excessive work and inhuman conditions, sometimes without proper food, housing or healthcare.

The piece says fear of not repaying debt, humiliation abroad, physical labour and mental distress make many ill; some die in workplace accidents and some take their own lives, leaving families with debt for many years.

headline_en: NID service launched at Bangladesh Embassy in Japan
summary_en: EC Senior Secretary Akhtar Ahmed inaugurated national ID (NID) services at the Bangladesh Embassy in Tokyo on 22 August 2025, so Bangladeshis in Japan can get NID services from the embassy. Applicants apply online at services.nidw.gov.bd and submit biometrics and documents at the embassy; he said arrangements are being made for postal ballot voting by expatriates in the next election.

facts.statement: On Friday 22 August 2025, Election Commission Senior Secretary Akhtar Ahmed inaugurated national ID (NID) services at the Bangladesh Embassy in Tokyo; Bangladeshis living in Japan can now get NID-related services from the embassy.
facts.source_in_article: Bangladesh Embassy Tokyo notice; EC Senior Secretary Akhtar Ahmed

facts.statement: To get an NID in Japan, apply online at https://services.nidw.gov.bd and then submit biometric data and the required documents at the Bangladesh Embassy in Tokyo.
NID online application website: https://services.nidw.gov.bd
Akhtar Ahmed said many Bangladeshis in Japan lack NIDs and therefore face problems getting many services at home.
EC Senior Secretary Akhtar Ahmed said (August 2025) arrangements are being made so that expatriates can vote by postal ballot in the next election.
Bangladesh's ambassador to Japan Md Daud Ali said the NID service fulfils a long-standing demand of Bangladeshis in Japan.
